section.title: Guides
section.meta_title: Shtil VPN guides — installing, internals, common questions
section.description: Step-by-step guides and plain explanations: Android TV without a browser, iPhone via a third-party client, why local sites break under a VPN, what VLESS + Reality and the sing-box core actually do, and the Windows and macOS install prompts.
section.lead: Walkthroughs and explanations. Only the things people actually ask us about.

articles.title: Installing a VPN on Android TV when the box has no browser
articles.description: Step by step: the Downloader app, a short remote-friendly address, what the system will ask, and how to finish the install with a remote. Plus why a TV needs the 32-bit build.
articles.lead: Android TV sets and boxes usually have no browser, and the app store does not show what is not in it. The file goes in through a downloader app — the standard route on that system. Typing the address with the remote is no longer needed: there is a numeric code, and with an Android phone nearby nothing is typed on the remote at all.

list: An Android TV set or box — version 6.0 or newer.
The remote. A mouse and keyboard are not required, but they are faster.
Any downloader app from your TV store. Downloader by AFTVnews is the most common one and is available almost everywhere. It is easier to find by voice — the remote has a microphone button.
A phone nearby — handy for opening the bot and showing the TV a code.

steps: Open the store on your TV and install Downloader if it is not there yet. Saying the name out loud beats typing it with the remote.

Launch it and click the address bar at the top: it takes both a code and an address. Type 7962408 and press «Go». If digits are easier, the «#» button to the right of the bar opens a number pad. The pad exists precisely for TVs: a code is four times quicker than an address, because it has no dots, no slash and no letters.
The file downloads on its own. The system asks once for permission to install apps from this source — grant it to the downloader app.
Then Google shows a red verification screen. It is the standard warning for any file from outside the store; the button you need is «Install anyway», at the bottom, reachable with the remote.
Open Shtil and press «Try now» — two hours run straight away, with no Telegram and no email.
For a permanent key take the linking code from the bot: the TV shows a field for a short code and the phone shows the code as a picture. The key arrives by itself.

blocks.h2: With an Android phone nearby: nothing typed on the remote
p: Install the free «Send files to TV» app on the phone, and on the TV from the very same place: in Google Play on the phone press the arrow next to «Install» and tick your TV. The remote stays on the table.
Download our file to the phone from sub.ndvsdom54.ru/get, open «Send files to TV», pick the file and tap the name of your TV. On the TV only arrows and «OK» are left.
The phone and the TV must sit on the same home network. A guest network with device isolation breaks this route — fall back to the code then.

blocks.h2: Why the TV gets the 32-bit build
p: TV boxes are overwhelmingly 32-bit, even recent models. The remote-friendly address always serves the 32-bit build: it runs everywhere, while the 64-bit one simply refuses to install on half of them.
Installing on a phone instead? Use the main button on the home page — it picks the right build for your device automatically.

blocks.h2: If the downloader rejects the address
p: If the code does not go through, type the full address: sub.ndvsdom54.ru/tv.apk — it leads to the same file and depends on nothing.
Downloader dislikes addresses that start with «https://» — type the string exactly as shown, starting at «sub».
Some firmwares block installs from a downloader app until «unknown source» is allowed for that very app in the security settings. The permission is granted once and stays.

blocks.h2: The app is installed — what now
p: One button connects. While the tunnel is up, local sites stay on the direct route — which matters on a TV, because built-in services and firmware updates go straight out and stay fast.
Updates are found by the app itself: when a new version appears, it offers to install it on the same screen.

articles.title: iPhone: adding the subscription to a third-party client
articles.description: We ship no iPhone build of our own — the subscription works in any client on the same core. Walkthrough with v2RayTun: where the link goes, which settings matter and which to leave alone.
articles.lead: There is no iPhone build from us: publishing to the App Store requires a company, not a person. The subscription link, however, is a standard one and opens in any client running the sing-box or Xray core.

p: The bot has a «My VPN» button that hands you a subscription link — a single line starting with https://sub.ndvsdom54.ru/sub/… That is what goes into the client.
A subscription link beats a bare key: when server settings change, the app pulls the new ones itself and nothing has to be re-shared.

steps: Install v2RayTun from the App Store.
Copy the subscription link from the bot.
In the app tap «+» → «Add from clipboard». The client parses the link and loads the profile.
Select the profile and tap connect. iOS asks once for permission to add a VPN configuration — a system prompt, and the tunnel will not come up without it.
Verify it works: open any foreign site, then any local one — the second should load exactly as fast as it did without the VPN.

list: Do not push your own routing rules into it: v2RayTun has built-in ones that work, and it silently ignores custom deep links and headers.
Do not change the TLS fingerprint. For Reality on iPhone it must be chrome — with safari the connection drops, which has been confirmed more than once.
Do not keep two VPN profiles active at once: iOS gives the tunnel to one of them, and the other will show «connected» while doing nothing.

p: Check the boring things first: subscription expiry in the bot, low-power mode, and iCloud Private Relay — the last one conflicts with the tunnel.
Re-creating the profile from the link helps more often than it should: clients cache old settings longer than you expect.
One key serves two devices at the same time. If the iPhone is the third one, connections will keep breaking — disconnect a device you no longer use.

articles.title: Why banks and government sites break when the VPN is on
articles.description: The actual cause: the site sees a foreign address and raises its defences. How a split route works on the device itself, and why the address lists have to live inside the app.
articles.lead: This is the single most common complaint about any VPN: you switch it on and your bank asks for extra confirmation, the government portal refuses you, the marketplace shows different prices. The cause is simple, and the fix is not «turn the VPN off».

p: An ordinary VPN pushes every packet through the tunnel. A local site then sees a request from a foreign address and does exactly what it was built to do: raises its defences, demands extra confirmation, sometimes refuses outright.
This is not about VPNs being banned. To a bank, a login from another country is a sign of a stolen account, and reacting to it is its job.

The route splits on the device itself: foreign addresses go through the encrypted tunnel, local ones go straight out as if the VPN were off. The site sees you at home, speed does not drop, extra checks never fire.
Shtil does this out of the box, but the technique is general — in clients built on the sing-box core it is called route splitting.

list: The lists of local domains and addresses must ship inside the app. Many clients fetch them at startup — and the server holding those lists is often unreachable from the very country that needs them, so the VPN never comes up at all.

For domains on the direct route, only the IPv4 address should be answered. Otherwise the device slips around the split via IPv6 and the site still sees a foreign visitor — the quietest failure of the lot.

steps: Connect.
Open a site that reports your public address — it should show a foreign one.
Immediately open a local site that guesses your city — it should place you at home.
If both say «abroad», the split is not working and everything is going through the tunnel.

articles.title: VLESS and Reality in plain words
articles.description: How VLESS differs from older protocols, what Reality does with the TLS handshake, and why such a node has no certificate of its own. No formulas.
articles.lead: Two words you meet in every modern key. Here is what each one does — enough to understand what you were handed and why it is configured this way.

blocks.h2: VLESS is transport with nothing extra
p: VLESS carries your data and deliberately does nothing beyond that: no encryption of its own, no heavy headers. Encryption is handled by the TLS layer above it.
The practical result is lower overhead — a lighter, faster connection, which shows most on weak hardware such as TV boxes.

blocks.h2: Reality is a way to look like an ordinary site
p: A normal secure endpoint presents a certificate of its own, and that certificate makes it easy to recognise. Reality takes another path: while establishing the connection it borrows the handshake of a real third-party site that you name in the settings.

From the outside it looks like an ordinary visit to that site. Such a node has no certificate at all — so nothing expires, nothing needs renewing, and there is no distinguishing mark to match against.

blocks.h2: What the fields in a key mean
list: sni — the name of the site whose handshake is borrowed.
pbk — the public half of the server key; the client uses it to confirm it is talking to the right node.
sid — a short identifier separating clients on one node.
fp — which browser your client imitates. On iPhone it is always chrome; with safari the connection drops.
flow — the transfer mode; in our keys it is what lets data pass without an extra wrapping layer.

blocks.h2: Why this is not just another protocol
p: The difference is not speed, it is how the connection looks from outside. Older protocols were recognisable by a characteristic pattern — a problem anywhere the network is picky about unfamiliar traffic.
Reality does not invent a new pattern; it borrows one that is already ordinary. That is the whole idea.

articles.title: What sing-box is and why the app is built on it
articles.description: The sing-box core: what it does inside a client, how it differs from its predecessors, how its config is shaped, and why the core ships inside the app instead of being downloaded.
articles.lead: sing-box is an open-source core that does the actual work: it holds the tunnel, reads the routing rules and decides where each request goes. The app around it is the screens, the buttons and the link to the bot.

list: Speak several protocols from one core — VLESS, Trojan, Shadowsocks and others, without a separate program for each.
Split routes by rule: domain, address, country, or a specific app on the device.
Raise a system-wide tunnel that carries every program's traffic, not just the browser's.
Resolve names itself — which matters, because a plain name lookup leaks half of your privacy.

blocks.h2: Why the core ships inside the app
p: Many clients download the core and the routing lists on first launch. That works beautifully until the day the address they download from stops answering: the app is then empty and will not connect.
Ours are compiled in. The internet is needed for the connection itself and nothing else — install and it works, even when third-party addresses are unreachable.
A sing-box configuration is a plain JSON file: inbounds, outbounds, routing rules. The subscription serves a ready-made one, and the app only adjusts local ports in it.
That is also what makes the subscription portable: the same address opens in any client on the same core — desktop, phone or TV box.
sing-box is distributed under GPL-3.0 with open sources. Our desktop app is open too; both repositories are linked in the footer of the home page.

articles.title: A subscription link instead of a key: why
articles.description: How a subscription link differs from a bare key, why nothing has to be moved by hand when settings change, and how one address serves phone, TV and desktop at once.
articles.lead: A key is one line describing one connection. A subscription link is an address where that line lives and keeps itself current. The difference looks small right up until the first time server settings change.

list: Server settings changed — devices pull the new ones themselves, and nothing has to be re-sent to anybody.
One address covers all of your devices: phone, TV, desktop.
The expiry date travels with the settings, so the app can honestly show how much time is left.
You never type it: the TV reads it off your phone's screen, the desktop takes a short code from the bot.

p: In the bot, the «My VPN» button. The bare key sits there too, behind a separate button — it is rarely needed, mostly for clients that do not understand subscriptions.
The two-hour trial is taken inside the app with no Telegram at all: it issues a temporary subscription on the same principle.
Two at the same time per key. That is not a limit on installs: put the app on five devices if you like — the limit counts simultaneous connections.
A third device does not get a clean refusal; instead connections start breaking for one device, then another. If your link feels unstable, first check whether an old phone is still connected.

articles.title: «Windows protected your PC»: what it is and what to press
articles.description: The SmartScreen prompt for apps without a publisher certificate: why it appears, how a certificate differs from actual safety, and how to get through it in two clicks.
articles.lead: The blue window looks alarming while saying something quite modest: «I am seeing this program for the first time». Here is where it comes from and what to press.

steps: In the blue window click «More info» — the link is inconspicuous on purpose.
A «Run anyway» button appears. Click it.
The installer then behaves normally, and the prompt will not come back on later launches.

p: Windows does not judge the contents of a program; it judges its reputation — how many people have already run this exact file, and whether it carries a publisher certificate. A new program has no reputation by definition.

We did not buy a publisher certificate. Since 2024 instant trust is not for sale anyway: the rules tightened, and reputation is still earned through install counts. We would rather explain the prompt in plain words than charge the subscription for it.

blocks.h2: How to check the file if you are uneasy
list: Download only from our address or the releases page — file names are permanent and do not change between versions.
Any file can be checked with free online scanners that run dozens of antivirus engines at once.
The desktop app's sources are open, and the build is produced from them in public.

p: Once installed, the app checks for new versions itself and installs only what is signed with our own key. So you see the prompt exactly once — at first install.

articles.title: macOS refuses to open an app from outside the App Store
articles.description: Gatekeeper and the quarantine flag: how «developer cannot be verified» differs from «the app is damaged», and how to open the program the supported way in two steps.
articles.lead: macOS will not allow the first launch of a program downloaded outside the App Store. This is expected behaviour, and there is a supported button for it — nothing needs to be broken.

steps: Try opening the app with a normal double click. The system refuses — as designed.
Open System Settings → Privacy & Security.
Scroll to the bottom: a line about the blocked app appears, with an «Open Anyway» button.
Click it and enter the administrator password. From then on the app opens with a double click and the question does not return.

blocks.h2: Two different messages — do not confuse them
list: «Developer cannot be verified» — the ordinary case: the app is signed but not notarised by Apple. The button above handles it.

«The application is damaged and should be moved to the Bin» — a different thing: there is no signature at all and the browser attached a quarantine flag. In that case the system shows no override button.

blocks.h2: What to do about the second one
p: Download a current build from our address: since August 2026 macOS builds are signed with our own key and this message no longer appears.

There are two Mac builds — Apple silicon and Intel. The browser does not reveal which one you need, which is why the page shows two buttons; if the app will not start, check that you took the right build first.

blocks.h2: Why the app is not in the App Store
p: Only a company can publish there, not a private person. So the file is served directly, and the app finds its own updates, installing only what is signed with our key.

articles.title: Why the app asks for VPN permission, and what it grants
articles.description: The system connection request: why it cannot be skipped, how a tunnel differs from a system proxy, and why the desktop app sometimes asks for administrator rights.
articles.lead: The first time you connect, the system asks for permission — a dialog on the phone, an admin prompt on the desktop. Here is what you are actually granting.

p: Android lets no app touch another app's traffic on its own. To route it through a tunnel, an app has to register with the system as a VPN — and the system shows a "Connection request" dialog naming the app.
You are asked once. While the permission holds, a key icon stays in the status bar — that is the system reminding you a tunnel is up. You can revoke it in Android settings, in the VPN section.

list: System proxy — the app opens a local endpoint and writes it into Windows or macOS settings. Everything that reads system settings goes through it: browsers, stores, most apps. No administrator rights needed.

Tunnel — traffic goes through a network interface the app creates, so everything goes through it, including software that knows nothing about proxies. Creating that interface is a system-level operation, which is why administrator rights are asked once.

blocks.h2: What the permission does not do
p: VPN permission covers network packets and nothing else. Files, contacts, camera, microphone and other apps' contents stay closed — the system has separate permissions for those, and the app does not request them.
On Android the app also asks for notification permission. That is for exactly one thing: the stop button in the notification shade, so you can drop the tunnel without opening the app.

articles.title: Key or subscription link: what to move to a new device
articles.description: How a vless:// string differs from a subscription link, why a new phone is better set up with the subscription, and how many devices work at once.
articles.lead: The bot hands you two things: a subscription link and a key as a plain string. They look different because they do different jobs — and on a new device you notice immediately.

list: Subscription link — an address the app fetches a ready configuration from: server, encryption and routing rules in one go.
Key — a single string holding the server address and connection parameters. It carries no routing rules.

blocks.h2: Why a new device is better set up with the subscription
p: A subscription refreshes: the app re-reads it and picks up current settings. If the server moves or the rules change, you re-enter nothing.

A key is a snapshot taken at the moment it was issued. It keeps working while the address holds, but routing has to be set up in the client by hand. That is the usual reason people report local sites and banks going through the tunnel.

steps: Open the bot and take the subscription link — it is the same one for all of your devices.
In our app you do not have to type it: the bot shows a pairing code and a QR, and the app reads it and configures itself.
The plain key sits next to it under its own button — you need it for third-party clients that do not understand subscriptions.

p: Two simultaneous connections per account. That is not a limit on how many devices you may install the app on, but on how many are connected at the same moment: a phone and a desktop work together, a third connection starts pushing the others off.

articles.title: Why the app is the size it is
articles.description: What makes up the download: the core shipped inside the package, routing lists compiled in, and per-processor builds instead of one universal file.
articles.lead: The Windows installer is 18 MB, the phone build is 26 MB, and the universal Android file is 72 MB. Here is where that comes from.

blocks.h2: Most of it is the core
p: The app window itself is small. The bulk is the sing-box core — the program that actually holds the connection. On desktop that is a separate file of roughly 45 MB, shipped inside the package and unpacked on install.

Shipping the core inside is a deliberate choice: the app works right after installation and downloads nothing on first run. "Fetch the core later" is smaller on disk right up until the moment there is nowhere to fetch it from.

Split routing relies on address lists: what goes direct and what goes through the tunnel. Many clients pull those lists from the network at startup. Ours are compiled into the app — an unreachable list should never stand between you and a working connection.

list: A build for your own processor — 26–28 MB. For most phones that is arm64.
The universal build — 72 MB: it carries every core variant at once. It helps when the processor is unknown, which is common for TV boxes and set-top devices.
App stores usually hide this difference by shipping only the part your device needs. We hand out files directly, so we show them all.

articles.title: Speed dropped: what to check before writing to support
articles.description: A short order of checks: compare against a direct connection, read the log and the connection list on the diagnostics screen, restart the core, check which mode is on.
articles.lead: "It got slow" comes from different places — a busy link, a saturated network, or a mode sending more traffic through the tunnel than needed. Check in this order.

blocks.h2: Separate the tunnel from the network
steps: Measure the speed with the app off. If it is low as well, the network or the plan is the answer and the tunnel is not involved.
Try local sites: they go direct, outside the tunnel. Slow there too — again the network.
If only foreign sites crawl while local ones fly, keep going down this list.

p: The desktop app has a Diagnostics screen with the working log and the list of current connections. That list shows what actually goes through the tunnel — now and then the culprit turns out to be one program pulling an update.

Connections are long-lived, and after a network change — home Wi-Fi to mobile data, say — an old session sometimes hangs around. The restart button on the main screen brings the core back up, which is faster than rebooting the machine.

list: System proxy — only software that reads system settings goes through the tunnel.
Tunnel — everything goes through it. It is the heavier mode, and on older hardware the difference shows.
If none of that helps, write to support and attach the app log — it shows where things break.

articles.title: Which macOS build to take: Apple silicon or Intel
articles.description: How to check your Mac's processor in ten seconds, what separates the two files, and why Homebrew removes the choice entirely.
articles.lead: We publish two files for macOS. They differ by the processor they are built for, and mixing them up is annoying rather than dangerous.

steps: Apple menu in the top left corner → "About This Mac".
Read the "Chip" or "Processor" line. "Apple M…" means Apple silicon. "Intel Core…" means Intel.
Download the file marked accordingly.

blocks.h2: If you take the wrong one
list: The Intel build on Apple silicon runs through the built-in compatibility layer — slower and noticeably heavier on battery.
The Apple silicon build on Intel will not start at all: the system reports the app as unsupported.
Either way it is reversible: remove the app, install the right file, and your settings and key are still there.

blocks.h2: When there is nothing to choose
p: Installed through Homebrew, the processor is detected for you and the right build is fetched — updates included.

articles.title: How this app differs from Hiddify and Throne
articles.description: Factual differences between a universal client and a single-service app: where the configuration comes from, what happens without an account, where updates arrive from.
articles.lead: Hiddify and Throne are universal clients: you paste any service's subscription into them. Our app is built around one service. Every difference follows from that.

list: In a universal client you paste a link or a key, and set up routing yourself if you want it.
Here the configuration arrives ready-made: server, encryption and split-routing rules are already assembled, and a pairing code from the bot is all the input there is.

blocks.h2: Before paying, and without an account
p: Our app has guest access: two hours of use with no Telegram and no sign-up, so you can see how it behaves on your own network. A universal client with no third-party subscription does nothing — it has nothing to connect to.

list: The app checks for new versions itself and installs only builds signed with our key.
The interface is translated into five languages — the same set the bot speaks.
Routing lists are compiled into the app rather than fetched at startup.

p: All three run the same core underneath: sing-box. That is why our subscription link works in the other clients too — if Hiddify or Throne is what you are used to, installing our app is optional.

articles.title: What goes into the app log, and what does not
articles.description: Where the log lives, what gets written, how long it is kept, and why no usage statistics leave the app.
articles.lead: The app keeps a working log — it is what makes breakage explainable. Here is what is in it and who gets to see it.

list: Working events: core start and stop, settings applied, connectivity checks, errors with their text.
The app's own network calls — a reachability check, a request for the current version.

The core's log, in a separate file: it shows the addresses the core handles. That is effectively a list of the sites and services your device reached, so keep it in mind before sending the log to anyone.

blocks.h2: Where it lives and how long
p: The log stays on the device, in the app's own folder, one file per day. Old files are cleaned up by the app so nothing piles up.
You can read it without leaving the app, on the Diagnostics screen.
Nowhere. The app carries no analytics, no usage counters and no crash-reporting service — the log stays on your device until you decide to send it.
If you do write to support about a fault, the log shortens the work considerably: it shows the exact step where things stop.

articles.title: Removing the app completely
articles.description: The full removal order on Windows, macOS and Android, where settings are left behind, and what happens to the subscription afterwards.
articles.lead: A normal uninstall takes the app away but leaves settings in place. If you want everything gone, here is the full order.

steps: Turn the tunnel off in the app and close it, otherwise some files stay locked.
Settings → Apps → "ShtilVPN" → "Uninstall".
Two settings folders remain. Open Explorer, paste %LOCALAPPDATA%\ShtilVPN into the address bar and delete the folder, then do the same with %APPDATA%\app.realityvpn.desktop.
If the app came from Scoop, one command covers all of it: scoop uninstall -p shtil-vpn.

p: Through Homebrew a single command does everything: brew uninstall --zap --cask shtil-vpn — it removes the app together with its settings.
Installed from the disk image, drag the app to the Trash, then delete ~/Library/Application Support/ShtilVPN and the app's files in ~/Library/Caches and ~/Library/Preferences.
A normal uninstall, same as any app: long-press the icon → "Uninstall". Settings go with it, and the system drops the VPN permission by itself.

Removing the app neither cancels the subscription nor deletes your key — it stays with the bot. Install the app again, or open the key in another client, and everything keeps working until the paid period ends.
